utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. We are now hearing the case of General Blaskic, please bring in the accused. (The accused entered court) Very well. Let us resume with the course of our work which was interrupted. This was because of a lack of a courtroom available to us. We hope that very shortly this will be remedied. Now, let us try then to resume with our good habits and be very brief with our examination-in-chief and with a brief cross-examination as well. Let us then resume. Mr. Cayley is going to begin the presentation of a witness. Mr. Blaskic, do you hear me, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I know everything else is in order to let us begin right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. The next witness is a Lieutenant-Colonel Reme Landry, who is a career army officer in the Canadian Armed Forces and was a member of the European Community Monitoring Mission from February of 1993 until August of 1993, occupying a number of positions in that organisation, finally leaving as deputy head of mission, directly under Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault of France. This witness will speak on a number of matters. I warn the court now that this will be a lengthy examination-in-chief. I apologise for that, but the Colonel has a lot of say. I will compress it as much as I possibly can. Indeed, there are a number of matters which other witnesses have spoken of which I will not include in his testimony. I will move it along as quickly as I can, but it will be a lengthy examination-in-chief. The witness will speak briefly at the start of his testimony about his training in Zagreb and information that was transmitted to him by the information cell of the European Community Monitoring Mission. He will then move on to his time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where he was a member of the Busovaca Joint Commission. You will recall an organisation set up in Busovaca by the international community, by UNPROFOR and ECMM in order to facilitate normalisation of life in the Lasva Valley by demilitarising, introducing cease-fires, reducing tensions between the HVO and Bosnian Army, investigating complaints of breaches of humanitarian law in the area. Colonel Landry was an active participant in that Commission and has a number of very important things to say about events which he witnessed as part of that Commission. He will give two examples of its work. He will speak to the court of an investigation into events in the village of Skradno in the municipality of Busovaca and this will be evidence of persecution and attempted forced transfer of Bosnian Muslim civilians from that village. He will then speak of the implementation of a cease-fire in the town of Busovaca and through this demonstrate to the court the command and control structures of the HVO and indeed the BiH through from superior units to subordinate units, and in fact the command and control structures were working effectively in both armies. He will then relate an account to you of an old Croatian couple he reunited in the village of Solakovici and demonstrate through this testimony his understanding of the situation on the ground that ordinary people had co-existed extremely well in the Lasva Valley until the outbreak of the conflict. He will give his views on how he believed the conflict developed. He will then speak generally on the attitude and the cooperation of the Bosnian army and the HVO to cease-fire agreements, to the implementation of the orders of the international community in the region. He will briefly speak of his knowledge of the communication systems of both the HVO and the Bosnian Army. He will then move on in his testimony and speak of events in the town of Travnik on 12th and 13th April and what he perceived as HVO provocation in that area and, indeed, he will speak of the Bosnian Army response to that provocation. He will speak of the removal of the mayor of the town, a Muslim, and how there was a general increase in tension in the area. He will then subsequently speak of a kidnapping of four HVO staff officers, a matter you heard evidence about previously. He was intimately involved in this process. This was a complaint that was made by the HVO to the Busovaca Joint Commission. He investigated it, and he subsequently secured the release of those four staff officers. He will give you the background as to why this event took place; the reasons behind it. He was in Vitez on the morning of 16th April. Very briefly, he will speak about what he saw of the HVO offensive in the town of Vitez on 16th April. He also saw Ahmici in flames that evening as did a number of other witnesses. He will speak to that briefly, then give more generally his professional opinion on the nature of that military operation; its scale, its organisation, how it would have been managed in a military sense. He will then speak on 18th April of a protest made jointly by the then Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic and Mr. Kostroman about atrocities allegedly committed against Bosnian Croats in the Zenica municipality. He will explain how he, along with the Bosnian army, who cooperated in an investigation, how he investigated those events and how he found, yes, that there had been atrocities committed against Bosnian Croats but about how those allocations had been grossly exaggerated by the HVO. He will speak of how the Bosnian Army attempted to secure the area, attempted to secure these Bosnian Croats civilians and indeed the Muslims living there, in order to try and reduce breaches of humanitarian law which were taking place. Conversely, he will explain to you how the HVO provided no cooperation whatsoever into an investigation into what happened in Ahmici. Indeed, he will speak, in his view, of a cover-up, an inability on behalf of the international community to investigate, and how ultimately a semi-forced entry had to be made into the village by the international community in order to find out what had taken place. He will confirm that absolutely no report was produced by the HVO in investigation into the events of Ahmici during his time in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He will speak about his perception of the removal of the deputy commander of the HVO, Franjo Nakic, just prior to the events in Ahmici. Franjo Nakic is a man Colonel Landry will speak well of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is all very well, but you seem to be repeating your summary. It is very well, but I am not asking for you to enter your plea now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will move ahead as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Be more objective, please. It is not a question of being too quick or going quicker, you are giving us now a summary and we appreciate that, but I am asking that you not go into presenting what is your own opinion, even if this is your own witness. I will make the same objection to the Defence if that were to arise. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He will speak of his opinion of the removal of the deputy commander of the HVO just prior to the operation that took place in Vitez and Ahmici on 16th April and he will give his views surrounding what he, Colonel Landry, perceived as a removal of that man. He will then speak of the setting up of the joint operation centre in Travnik on 20th April 1993. Again, another attempt by the international community to normalise the situation in the Lasva Valley. He will explain how Franjo Nakic reappeared, this time as chief of staff of the HVO, in a different position, on this particular Commission and Colonel Landry will speak of his views about Mr. Nakic's position on that Commission. Next, he will speak of incidents on 21st April in the Kiseljak municipality and the visits again by the international community, specifically by him to the village of Rotilj and Colonel Landry will provide eye-witness testimony as to what he saw during that time. Next we will move on to the mid-May period, where Colonel Landry will explain to the court a change in the tactical situation on the ground. At this stage, the HVO were on the defensive. In fact, the Bosnian Army were now placing pressure on the Vitez pocket. Colonel Landry will explained how that changed the situation within the Vitez pocket. He will then speak, in June of 1993, as to the events surrounding the Tuzla convoy. He will explain to the court how that convoy was ransacked by the HVO in the Vitez municipality. He will explain to the court his reasoning behind his view that this was an organised attack on a convoy by the HVO. He will finally speak to you of his views about the influence of the Vance-Owen Plan on what had happened in Central Bosnia and, indeed, throughout territory controlled by the HVO. You will remember, as I said earlier, he was deputy head of Mission; he was receiving reports and, indeed, witnessing events on the ground so he had a very good grasp of events through the country. He will also speak of HV, Croatian army involvement, in the conflict between the HVO and the BiH in Bosnia-Herzegovina, both through reports he was receiving and through eye-witness testimony. Finally, your Honours, he will give you his considered opinion on the accused's responsibility for the events which took place in Central Bosnia. This is opinion; it is the opinion of a professional soldier, and it is based on experience as an eye-witness testimony of the events as they took place during April through to August of 1993. Finally, the evidence he will give -- if you wish I can indicate to you the relevance to the indictment -- it is relevant to paragraphs 1, 3 and 4, which relate to the background and the superior authority; paragraphs 5, 5.1 and 5.2; paragraph 6, 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.6 and 6.7, which is the persecution count; paragraph 8, which is the unlawful attack charge; paragraph 9, which is wilful killing; paragraph 10, which is counts 11 to 13, destruction and plunder of property. Paragraph 11, which is count 14, destruction of institutions dedicated to religion and education. Finally, paragraphs 12 and 13, which is relevant to counts 15 and 20. In the course of my examination-in-chief, I will bear in mind, Mr. President, what you have previously advised us about the manner in which it is to be conducted. I may well be asking more questions, leading in a manner which is acceptable to the Defence, in order to direct the testimony. Otherwise we will be here for weeks with this witness. If that is acceptable, if we could call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see that from my colleagues that everything is in order, so we can indeed ask the Registrar to bring in Mr. Landry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In response to the request by my learned counsel, we certainly do not object to directing the witness to a particular subject-matter, although I do not understand why there would be a need to lead the witness with respect to his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is an observation which I think is unnecessary, because it is for the judges to decide whether or not they are leading questions that are being put to the witness. (The witness entered court) Do you hear me, Colonel? Now, could you please remind us of your name, and your rank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Reme Landry, I am a Lieutenant-Colonel in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing while we ask you to take the solemn declaration. This is what is going to be read to you by the bailiff. LIEUTENANT-COLONEL LANDRY (Sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, Colonel, please be seated. The Prosecutor has already given us a summary, but dense summary, of what will be contained in your testimony. Following that, and before questions put to you by Mr. Cayley, you should understand that from time to time the Prosecution may come in to help make this testimony more concise and, as you know, you also will be subject to a cross-examination later on by the counsel for the accused, Mr. Blaskic, who is present here today in the courtroom. Without any further delay, we will carry on this session until 6.30. We will resume, of course, tomorrow in the start of the afternoon. Mr. Cayley, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Landry, I understand that most of the work you carried out in Bosnia-Herzegovina was done in the English language and there may be from time to time the need for you to speak in English, although you will be testifying in French for the bulk of your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is about right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, do not discourage the witness from perhaps expressing himself in French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With your permission, your Honour, I would simply like to add to what Mr. Cayley just said. Indeed, most of my work was carried out in the language of Shakespeare and indeed, I have written in the language of Shakespeare, I want this to be understood; perhaps from time to time I may express myself in the language of Moliere as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Express yourself in the language which you find to be most efficient in your testimony. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the first document could be presented to the court, which is Exhibit 282. You will be pleased to hear, Mr. President, this is a document which is only in French. There is no translation in English. (Handed). Now, Colonel Landry, this is your resume and I do not intend for you to read it to the court. If I could just very briefly sum-up its essence, you are a Canadian citizen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think in 1973, you were commissioned into the Royal Vandous Regiment in the Canadian army after five years at the Royal Military College in Montreal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are, I think, by specialisation, a professional infantry officer and you have done almost every job in the army that an infantry officer can do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think in your career you have been responsible in a command position for up to 600 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you are also airborne trained and you were chief instructor at the Canadian Infantry Training School?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can specify. I am not a pilot, but I am a parachutist. The rest is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In essence, I think you have been 30 years in the Canadian army and you have served in Canada and Germany with NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In 1997, you completed an MSc in political science at the University of Montreal and I think the subject of this thesis was the true origin of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I received a Masters in political science in that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the microphone will actually pick up your voice without you needing to lean forward. Your testimony today, however, will be based on your eye-witness experience in Bosnia and, indeed, the reports that were produced by ECMM and other documents which you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have a number of medals on your chest, I think including the Order of Military Merit, which -- I do not wish to embarrass you, but I think is one of the highest medals which can be awarded in peace time to an Canadian officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not a medal for courage, rather it is a medal given to members of the military population in Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, if we can move to the essence of your testimony. Am I right in saying that you were sent as an ECMM Monitor to Bosnia-Herzegovina at the end of February 1993 by the Canadian government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Canada is not a member of the European Union. Can you explain to the court why Canada provided Monitors for the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, the European Community was pleased to receive those countries who wanted to participate in that mission, which included Canada, also Poland, Sweden, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, which also sent Monitors to participate in the Monitoring Missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the head of the ECMM in Zenica at that time was Jean-Pierre Thebault of France?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ambassador Thebault was the chief of the regional Zenica centre and not the ECMM chief. He was the chief of the regional centre of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you held a number of positions, including finally chief of operations and then, finally, deputy chief of Mission to Ambassador Thebault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during my stay in Bosnia, I worked under Ambassador Thebault, since that was the practice of the European Community; the newcomers had a short stay as Monitors and during this time, they could learn what they would have to do in order to occupy more senior positions, either in the Zagreb headquarters or in various regional sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I believe that you were given a brief in Zagreb prior to your arrival in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have to understand that most of the Monitors who had been sent to serve with the European Community had rather limited knowledge about the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. In addition to receiving information from our governments, when we arrived in the former Yugoslavia, at that point, we went through an apprenticeship that took place for several days at the headquarters in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 283, please? (Handed). Can you explain to the court the purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During this orientation period, to learn the procedures used by the ECMM Monitors, we had to be present at briefing sessions, during which the major belligerents, or at least the situation on site or on the ground, was explained to us in rather detailed fashion, based on various information and intelligence that the ECMM headquarters had at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to paragraph 27 of this document? If you could read that out to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The Croatian Defence Council, HVO, is believed to be controlled by the Croatian army from Zagreb. The HVO parade in two main areas, north Bosnia and west Herzegovina, with the HQ at Mostar and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now direct your attention to paragraph 33, and the third sentence of that paragraph. If you could read that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "They also have support from paramilitary, HOS, troops who are now being incorporated into the HVO as they have been into the HV in Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, those are fairly bold statements. Were they based on intelligence or information that had been gathered by the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to say "yes", in answer to your question, with a caveat, however, which is that it was information that had been analysed by the intelligence service of the ECMM and all information which received -- or that they received, tended to confirm what is stated in these paragraphs, as stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, these two views were views that were held throughout ECMM; they were no big secrets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this was no great secret, but you must understand that this information really was circulated within ECMM, it was not published in newspapers, or in other documents that might have been seen among others, by the belligerents in the conflict and the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, Colonel, moving on, you travelled quite widely in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If the witness could be shown at Exhibit 284, which is a map. (Handed). Now, the map in front of you, does this indicate the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina in which you spent the greatest amount of time? I imagine you must have travelled through others on journeys to various places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. You should understand that the regional centre of Zenica had the operational responsibility for all the territory under the control of the Bosnians, or at least the HVO. This was mainly within this vast territory that I worked during the six months that I was in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you had an understanding of events that were taking place in the majority of these municipalities that are shaded in on this map, at least in the sense of receiving reports, rather than direct evidence in all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it should be understood that most of my stay, that my residence was in Central Bosnia, but that from the time that I received higher positions, when I was named chief of operations, and deputy to Mr. Thebault, it was especially from that point on that I moved a bit more within Bosnia and I was, at that point, able to be in contact with various people and have different relations and have close contacts with various detachments, which composed the Zenica regional centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 285, and there is a translation of this document which is 285A. (Handed). The French translation, unfortunately, Mr. President, is not complete, but it will be. There are a couple of pages missing, but it will not affect the witness's testimony since he will be summarising the essence of these documents to the court. Now, Colonel Landry, if you could explain to the court, using these documents, the background to the Busovaca Joint Commission, the reason why it was set up and, in fact, its ultimate purpose in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should say that the establishment of the Busovaca Commission was carried out before I arrived. As you remember, I came in -- I arrived at the beginning of March, whereas this document that you have in front of you is dated February 1993. At that time, in February 1993, among the Bosnian Muslim and Croatian forces and the third Bosnian commander and the central operational zone, there was a cease-fire that had been decided on, and the cease-fire was more or less sponsored by the direct intervention of the European Community, through the Zenica regional centre. The cease-fire covered various sections in such a way that it allowed all of the population in Central Bosnia -- allowed them to return to a normal situation after the various conflicts and violence which had been initiated, according to what I was told, throughout -- in the winter of 1993. After the cease-fire agreement had been signed, and the commitment on the part of the various regional commanders, it was recognised that in order to be able to implement the various resolutions, at that point, there would have to be a Joint Commission with representatives of the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, as well as representatives from UNPROFOR, especially from BritBat, and a representation which had been presided over by the regional centre, so that everything would be carried out in an orderly manner and quickly, so that there would be an official podium were the various belligerents could speak or address their concerns in respect of the application of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit 286? (Handed). And if this could be placed on the ELMO? Now, Colonel, does this represent the structure of both the Busovaca Joint Commission and the Co-ordination Committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the structure that was in place when I arrived at the beginning of March -- when I arrived in Zenica, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you will see, under "Co-ordination Committee", it says: "CO BritBat, ECMM Chairman, Commander Bosnian Third Corps, Commander HVO central command." Now, the CO Britbat was Colonel Stuart; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you identify the other individuals, just down to and including the Joint Commission itself? You do not need to identify the teams who actually occupied the positions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Busovaca Commission was principally composed of two Corps: one which was called the Co-ordination Committee, which included, in regular fashion -- that would meet about once a month and which contained the major signatories to the cease-fire as well as the members of the working group or of the -- in Busovaca. This -- this Busovaca Committee had four sub-units. The sub-units included a representative of three ECMM representatives and, on the average, there were between three to six UNPROFOR representatives, depending upon the logistical needs we had for them. Each belligerent -- if I can use that word -- each representative of the BiH and HVO armies, also had between three to four and sometimes even five representatives. If you look at the agreement that was signed in February, you will see that some of the representatives were designated by their names and represented a specific field of activity, that they had a specific role to play within the Commission. But we must still say, and it is important to say, that the two deputy commanders, that is the deputy commander for the Third Corps, that is General Mr.dan, and the deputy commander of the HVO for the BiH -- HVO central operational zone, was Nakic. The Busovaca Committee would meet permanently, almost every day. Do you want me to go on with further details?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The two deputy commanders of the Bosnian Third Corps and the deputy commander of the HVO central command-- to which individuals were they reporting up the chain of command? And if you could name those two individuals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards General Mr.dan, he represented me and he would go directly to Azijananovic, who was the commander of the third camp. As regards Mr. Nakic, he reported directly to the commander of the operational Central Bosnia zone, that is General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What would the nature of the complaints that the Busovaca Joint Commission heard from both parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the complaints that we received dealt specifically with the implementation of the various agreements that had been signed on 13th February. You should understand that this Committee played two major roles: that is, they were in charge of monitoring the implementation of the various agreements which had been signed and, at the same time, they were supposed to be in a position to serve as a kind of neutral mediator for any complaints received either by the Third Corps or the HVO which represented the central operational zone. Therefore, if I can give you a quick description of a typical day of the Committee's work -- I could do that if you permit me to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just one last question: were there reports made by both sides of breaches of international humanitarian law, as you understood it as an army officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to explain to you. The way the procedures, or at least the way the Committee worked, was that in the morning we would begin with a report of requests that had been received the day before, after which, both the two groups of representatives would make comments or express complaints, having to do with the implementation of the agreement of 14th February. Then afterwards, during the day, we would be divided into two groups, so that we could investigate the nature of the complaints which had been made to us. After that, both senior representatives of the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats were to make a report to their headquarters; they were to investigate what had been said and then possibly to come back to the Commission in the following days in order to state what steps they wanted to take or what had been taken in order to remedy the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 287. (Handed). Together with the French translation, which is 287A. Now, very briefly, Colonel, if you could explain to the court what this document shows, as to the implementation of the earlier orders which you have presented to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Joint Committee would meet, this meant that the Busovaca Committee was to present to the Joint Committee a report on each of the sections which the cease-fire of 13th February was to cover. So, what you have in front of you is an example, from the beginning of April, which shows the progress which both factions had made over the preceding month insofar as the implementation of the agreements of 13th February are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could direct you to order 432, which is "return of people". If you could explain to the court the progress that had been made in that respect? That is, the return of individuals to their original home in the region.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As it is written in French, you have to understand that the conflicts which had taken place in Central Bosnia were conflicts which were not purely military but which implicated certain civilians. Some people had been displaced for security reasons, or had been saved for security reasons. Before one was able to implement fully all of the directions which had been signed, a climate of confidence had to be created in order to allow people to go back freely. You must understand that at that time there were not many institutions operating in Central Bosnia. The police were not terribly active. There was no justice system in place. The two military chiefs therefore represented, for all practical purposes the authority par excellence which predominated at the time, and that is why at that time we decided to come to this agreement in such a way that both the original chiefs would be able to initiate a series of procedures which would allow them to normalise the situation and which would allow them to gradually ensure that the situation would go back to normal. But you should understand the fact that we were aware of the fact that before allowing people to go back to their homes, other things had to be done first. So, what the report stated, among other things, was that we were not as successful as we would have hoped to have been and that the agreements of 13th February had not been fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if we could move ahead and briefly give an example of an investigation of a complaint on the Busovaca Joint Commission and specifically I want to refer to you the village of Skradno and the events which took place in that village in early March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of my first investigations involved the complaints which had been made by the Bosnian Muslims, saying that the small enclave in Skradno, which was very close to Busovaca, in which most of the people were Muslims, were complaining of harassment, of thefts, and they asked us to investigate this with a delegation from UNPROFOR -- that is HVO representatives and Bosnian Muslims -- with us. We went to investigate the nature of the complaints in that small village. I should tell you, and I remember very well, because it was the first experience that I had, the first -- the first practical investigation that I had carried out since my arrival in Bosnia. When I came into the village, this village which -- I could see that there were many women weeping and that is what impressed me. The village of Skradno was a little village of farmers. Most of the workers were women with children and then there was men as well. We were told that the village was mainly guarded by the police and by the HVO and that the people were not free to move about. There were regular thefts of automobiles, which was very inconvenient for the people and prevented some of them from going to work. People were not allowed to go freely to do work in their fields and, in addition to that, I actually was made aware of certain harassment complaints by certain women. These women told me that regularly people would come to bother them during the night, people who were dressed in black and who had masks and who would force the people to go out of their homes and there would be a kind of a fake execution, because at that point the people would be lined up against their homes and the people responsible for them would aim at them and fire at them but of course they would not be wounded. We could see that on two of the houses that there were obvious traces of bullets in the walls slightly above the heads of those people. So you understand that this created a very difficult climate for those people who were living there, and after that I was told that if the people wanted to leave the village of Skradno, they could do so, but so long as they would sign a piece of paper saying that they were doing it freely and that they would not come back to Skradno.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which authority was trying to make them sign this piece of paper to say that they were leaving voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I understood was simple. It was kind of a pocket of Muslims within a municipality which had an HVO predominant population. So the police or military units which surrounded the village were directly or indirectly under the control of the military HVO chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after you had investigated this complaint, did you speak to Franjo Nakic, the deputy commander of the HVO, about the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point, I do not think Mr. Nakic was with me when I went for the first visit, but since I mentioned his name before -- there was not only Mr. Nakic but other representatives of the HVO and those people were present with us when we would interrogate people and they would, afterwards, as a matter of course, make a report up the chain of command. Then, within a reasonable amount of time, they were supposed to show us what improvements had been made as to any problems which had been attributed to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it your view that whenever you -- or is it a fact -- that whenever you investigated this type of incident, that the matter was reported up the chain of command in the HVO and, indeed, the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was the very nature of the Commission and the agreement was that possibly whatever had been reported by the Commission should move along and be reported directly to the various headquarters of both forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I should imagine that in your time on the Commission, you investigated a significant number of these types of incidences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitively I did. In short, as I said to you, most of the afternoon, while we would deliberate, the days were really devoted to investigating the nature of the protest that we had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move on and the witness could be shown Exhibit 288, which is also translated into French as Exhibit 288A. (Handed). Could you explain to the court the nature of this document, your involvement in these events, and what conclusions it led you to believe about the chain of command in the HVO and the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in order to try to simplify the structure of both armed groups that we were faced with, the operational command of the HVO and of the Bosnian Muslims represented the operational level. Directly below them was what one could call a more military -- they were brigades which were directly responsible for some sectors of municipalities, and beneath each of the brigades was a series of what one could call "local commands", perhaps the equivalent of company or battalion commanders. Therefore, the work that we had to do explains the progression that we made. You should understand that the agreements of 13th February had been signed on the operational command level and their application was to take place on the level of the local commands. Therefore, the Commission worked in such a way that we possibly would it be able to meet with the brigade commands, then after that to meet the local commanders, so that, among other things, we would be able to maintain a cease-fire and so that we would be able to be sure that those people carried out what they had -- were to do. You should understand this was a rather unusual situation; that is, the belligerents had regrouped within various municipalities and there were kind of artificial dealings which had been created between these municipalities -- or that you could find in the same village you could find a village which would have a majority of Muslims or a majority of Croats and the two sections, because of the conflict, had established a kind of surveillance post, armed trenches with military equipment which really would survey -- amounted to one or another, almost 24 hours a day. Any kind of belligerency on the other part, the second party would respond by firing, then there sometimes would be people who were wounded, as a result of the exchange of fire. One of our tasks was to be sure that there would be better understanding and a better sharing of information between the commanders, so possibly one would be able to disengage them and to space out these trenches which allowed them to monitor one another. So, we wanted to move out the trenches which were what I could say were near -- right next to the belligerent parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, in fact, this report indicates that you were successful in ensuring that the two local commanders in Solakovici actually filled up their front-line positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You should understand that around 6th April, we were very optimistic, despite a rather difficult beginning, and we tried to regroup these people. At that time, we had to think a great deal; we had a mediate between the two groups of belligerents in order to facilitate the progression forward. But around 6th April we had had a lot of success and you should understand that these meetings took place regularly, either on the Bosnian -- on the Muslim or Croatian side, which meant that the local commanders had to be moved about. When originally this was done, we did this under armed escort -- the British took care of that, which allowed us to use our light vehicles in a more efficient fashion in order to transport people and around 6th April the local belligerents met without even any need for ECMM Monitors, because the relationships between them had become normalised and there was less and less breaches of cease-fires. You should understand those people were not enemies going back for many years, but frequently they were neighbours, they were people who had gone to the same schools, but for one reason or another had become enemies. Once we were able to initiate dialogue between them through frequent exchanges we were in a position to renew certain links of camaraderie which existed. I must say around 6th April, in my sector, which was the sector which was in the south-east of Busovaca, that is the Kacuni region, Trnpole and Gornji and Solakovici, I could say that the relations were excellent and we that were moving toward the achievement of what we were aiming at. But I would like to add, nonetheless, that there was a great deal of concern -- the local commanders wanted to have written orders from the brigade commanders in which it would be stated clearly, in writing, that they had to fill up the trenches. We had the orders from the operational level commanders saying that they accepted -- in fact, they gave the order that these trenches be filled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In fact, you have provided to the Prosecutor a copy of this order which, in the original language is Exhibit 289. The French translation is 289A and the English translation, which is a field translation, is 289B. If that could be shown to the witness. (Handed). Colonel, you stated that orders were required for these filling in of trenches to be required. Indeed, this level of command was two below the operational zone command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you are an army officer, what did this actually indicate to you about the chain of command, both in the HVO and the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It simply indicated there was a great deal of distrust on the part of the people and that people -- at least the belligerents on the battalion or company level -- did not want to be seen as having taken initiatives which might go against certain strategies of their own chains of command. Therefore, this meant that we needed these kinds of orders, despite the fact that we had already had a rather broad cease-fire. But the chain of command wanted to cover their own -- to protect themselves, to cover their own backs when they would fill up the trenches, and not be accused of treason. They really wanted it to be understood that they had received written orders. There was a great deal of distrust in regard to their own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now you stated that they required written orders because that might go against certain strategies of their own chain of command. Do you believe, in respect of the HVO, was the strategy of that chain of command not in synchronisation with these activities you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to admit to you that, starting in April, there was a type of situation which was difficult to explain and which was shared by all of these ECMM Monitors and by some other elements from the Zagreb headquarters, meaning that both on the local level, or on the level of those people on the ground who had goodwill and who wanted to normalise relations, it did seem that on the HVO level, as regards -- in respect of realisation of other agreements that they had signed, that any excuse could be used in order to delay the implementation. At that time, we should understand that at the end of March/beginning of April, the strategic situation of the Bosnian Army was very fragile. The Bosnian Army had to fight on two fronts, almost. The Serbs were more and more aggressive. This was at the time, you remember, there was a great deal spoken about security zones, safe zones and that there were reinforcement -- and resupply convoys, became less frequent for Bosnia. There was an enormous amount of difficulty for the Bosnians, they had more and more difficulty in maintaining the training -- maintaining the control -- the territory they controlled in one piece. They would -- it would seem later they were in a better position and it was clear that at that time, in Central Bosnia, for reasons having to do with better lines of communication, or better reinforcement, the HVO was in a strategically much stronger position than the Bosnians. Therefore, one could see at that time that as much as the local people wanted to normalise the situation, the strategy of the HVO wanted just as much to delay the implementation of the agreements. As much as one can say for -- to some extent one can say that the Bosnians tried by every means possible to meet their needs by adopting a very conciliatory attitude towards the HVO, or the HVO representatives, before they would implement some of the agreements which had been signed on 13th February.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the date of this particular order that was issued by both the Busovaca HVO brigade commander and the Busovaca Bosnian Army brigade commander? I think you will find it is 9th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is 9th April and 8th April. I think that the order, as such, could not be signed with both of the generals but when we were going from one brigade command -- I had to go another and one would sign and then the other; everything was done around the 8th and 9th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long after the original agreement which had been signed by Colonel Blaskic and Colonel Halilovic was this order given by the brigade commander in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You should understand that the first cease-fire or the original cease-fire was signed around 13th February, so, you see, everything was signed on 13th February and about six weeks later the brigade commanders gave written orders to their local commanders for the execution, among other things, of the filling up of the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What does that space of time indicate to you, the gap between the signing of the original order, and then the signing of this order on 9th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously, it shows that even though the original intentions were to implement the agreement of 13th February, in practice, the will was not fully present to actually implement the agreement on the cease-fire, because there was lack of confidence between the belligerents and they sought every possible way to reassure themselves that they would not do something that could have negative consequences during this period; particularly, those who were in a weaker position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move on to an incident in which you were involved in the village of Solakovici, where I think you reunited an old Bosnian Croat couple. I would like you to briefly to explain the facts of that incident to the court then, in fact, give your conclusions on those events, what those events indicated to you about the conflict that was taking place in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be said that when I arrived in Bosnian territory, I already had an understanding of the situation. I was convinced that we were facing an ethnic conflict, that the Catholics detested the Muslims and vice versa. During our meeting with local commanders, among others, in the small village of Solakovici, composed of both elements, Gornji Solakovici, which means "above" and Donji Solakovici is "below", the Muslims were concentrated in the upper part and the Croats were in the lower part. During the first meeting, held in Gornji Solakovici, when I escorted HVO representatives, an old Croat man came, crying, asking me to give certain objects to his wife, who, since the beginning of the conflict, had been separated from him. His wife had stayed behind in the house, the Muslim area, whereas he at that point in time was working with the people in the Croatian area and he wanted to have news of his wife. He did not know the conditions under which she was living. Therefore, I took the initiative to ask the Croatian representative whether there would be any problems if I took the old man, because I must tell you that -- whether I could take him with us, and so that he could, himself, see what the position of his wife was. So, to make a long story short, I managed to convince the Croats that we could leave this man with his wife. When I saw the warm welcome given to him by the Muslim villagers, the local Muslim commanders had no difficulty in allowing the old man to stay there with his wife. After that, I met them regularly. Everything seemed to be going fine. The people were happy, and I think that this was one of the occasions when I felt I was able to bring a little happiness to these people. Later on, the situation was aggravated, the conflicts resumed, and the people of Gornji Solakovici were isolated and one evening they were shelled and I was not able to visit them as frequently as I wanted. After another cease-fire, I was able to return to Gornji Solakovici to see that the old man was no longer there. He could not understand at all what was happening in his village. He could not understand that the people from below were shelling his Muslim friends and his wife found him about three or four o'clock in the morning hanging. The old lady wanted to stay there. She would not leave him. She was not able to give a funeral service for her husband. I am saying all this to tell you that this gave me the impression that the people did not understand what was happening. They could not understand that their friends -- age-old friends -- had become such bad people. There seemed to be a will beyond them, that forced these people to do things which they did not really always want to do; the local people did not want to do. From that moment, I understood it was not a war of religion in this corner of the country, but that it was something artificial; an attempt to provoke incidents and violence, hoping that eventually those incidents would encourage hate, revenge, and, thus result in control over people who hated one another, following the atrocities that were committed against their family members or friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated that you believed that the people in the villages had got along very well together and had previously got along very well together, but that there was an attempt to provoke incidences and violence between them. Who do you believe was actually behind that provocation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, it became evident that, for reasons of strategy which I may explain a little later, perhaps, there were numerous incidents that were provoked on the part of the HVO in order to provoke reaction from the Muslims and, eventually, to have every reason to be able to react against those reactions of those people. I must say that at that point in time it was important for the HVO, on the one hand, to be able to gain international support by signing such cease-fires and in March and the beginning of April to adhere to the Vance-Owen Plan, and the HVO was the first ethnic group to sign that Plan. On the one hand the signal was given to the international community that they were very interested in achieving conciliation and, on the other hand, one could see that behind the scenes there was another strategy that was being developed. They really wanted to consolidate their positions and, among other things, to make sure that the territories that would become Croatian territories, according to the Vance-Owen Plan, would be controlled fully by Croats and that the majority of Croats would remain within those provinces and they would do everything to facilitate or initiate the departure of Muslims so that they may go to Muslim areas and the Croats could come to Croatian areas. I can explain in greater detail with the help of maps, perhaps, my understanding of the situation as it was at that point in time in Central Bosnia; a situation that showed that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the importance that the centre in Mostar had, which was the HVO base at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, to finish this area of your testimony, how would you describe the degrees of cooperation of the HVO command and the Bosnian Army command in respect of the implementation of cease-fires and the related agreements? Can you give the court the reasons why -- if there was a difference in the approaches of the two commands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me repeat a little bit of what I said. It was not just my understanding, but the understanding of the whole regional centre of Zenica that we were facing a situation where the two sides did not look upon the situation from the same angle. The Bosniaks were in a situation to face two fronts; they wanted to have an agreement with the HVO so as to be able to use communication routes leading to Central Bosnia, because at the time HVO controlled the main routes leading to Central Bosnia for purposes of supplies, with food and ammunition and, on the other hand, it was apparent that the HVO had a tactical and strategic position which was far more favourable for them. They, on the other hand, wanted to use that position to be able to slow down, to their advantage, the implementation of these various cease-fire agreements so as to be able to exercise better control over the totality of provinces which would possibly come under Croatian control; the HVO control. It should also be said that at the same time there were -- non-written agreements, but agreements between certain HVO factions and Serb factions. This allowed the HVO to bring even stronger pressure to bear on the Bosnian party. Also, there were reports at the level of the Monitoring Mission where there was reference to a tacit agreement between Milosevic and Tudjmann regarding the possible division of Bosnia and that this division would probably be based on the Vance-Owen Plan and provinces that were designated as Croatian majority provinces would become Croatian. So that there appeared to be an attitude on the part of the HVO that was very intransigent with respect to the Bosniaks. It is also rather curious, but one has to know that at the same time, since the beginning of the conflict, there were HVO troops that were fighting side by side with the Bosniak forces in the north of Central Bosnia. At the time, the region of Tuzla, there were HVO troops which, from the beginning of the conflict, were able to support and fight on the Bosniak side against the Serbs. Therefore, this gave us an impression that, in fact, there was something rather bizarre going on, why the Croats or the HVO of Central Bosnia were so intransigent and delayed so much cooperation with the Bosniaks while, at the same time, the same HVO, the same Bosnian Croats in the north of Central Bosnia did not seek to avoid the Bosniaks but, on the contrary, joined the Bosniak forces to fight on a regular basis against the Serbs. The only way in which I could explain that was that there was some kind of an agreement somewhere and that it was a strategic decision that the HVO should be concentrated in the south of Bosnia, whereas the rest of the Bosniak territory would, perhaps, be given to the Serbs. That was the understanding or the only understanding that I was at that time able to give to events. My contacts with the local population -- and I had many -- showed me, once again, that these people were ready not to forget the past, but to cooperate. They wanted to stay in their houses; to live with Bosniak and their Croatian neighbours. Therefore, for me, and not just for me but the people I worked with, the only way for us to understand this attitude was that there must have been an HVO strategy which sought in every way to gain absolute control over Central Bosnia, so as, once it was accomplished, to be able to separate and divide Bosnia between them and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, this is an appropriate time to pause. We are moving into the next section of Colonel Landry's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I quite agree with you, Mr. Cayley. We will resume work tomorrow at 2.30. (6.30 pm)
